name: Samaaya
title: A Mathematical Comparison of Traditional Newari Wooden Windows and Mughal Jali Screens
verdictSummary: A strong topic with a genuine personal connection. Before you begin, the research question needs to become measurable and the mathematics needs more analytic depth to reach the AA SL top band.
strengths: Your personal connection is authentic — living in Nepal, surrounded by Newari architecture. Keep your own photographs and measurements at the centre of the work; that is exactly what the top of the personal-engagement criterion rewards.
The solid-to-void ratio is your strongest idea. It turns “these look different” into a single defensible number per screen — build the exploration around measurable comparisons like it.
Coordinate modelling in GeoGebra with the Shoelace formula for area is appropriate and clean.

revisions.label: Narrow to two specific, named artifacts.
revisions.text: You cannot do rigorous maths on whole traditions. Choose one specific Newari window (ideally one you can photograph yourself — name the building and place) and one named Mughal jali (e.g. from Fatehpur Sikri or the Sidi Saiyyed mosque). Do all the maths on those two objects.

revisions.label: Make the research question measurable, and state a hypothesis.
revisions.text: Replace “differences and similarities” with a question answered by computed quantities — e.g. how the two compare in rotational symmetry, angular construction, and void-to-solid ratio. Predict the Newari lattice is a rectilinear grid (low rotational order) while the jali uses high-order star-polygon symmetry, then test it.

revisions.label: Go deeper than polygons — decisive for your mathematics mark.
revisions.text: Derive angles with trigonometry rather than measuring them with a protractor; model the curved / cusped elements with functions and use integration for their areas; include one short piece of reasoning or proof (e.g. that a star motif’s outer points are concyclic). Treating everything as a polygon is the single biggest limiter on Criterion E.

revisions.label: Thread reflection throughout, not just at the end.
revisions.text: Address perspective distortion honestly — a photo of a window is rarely perfectly head-on, and this corrupts your void-ratio numbers; explain how you corrected or estimated the error. Also reflect on why carved stone versus jointed wood constrains the geometry differently.

revisions.label: Treat the Golden Ratio extension with caution.
revisions.text: Only include it if you test it honestly (state the measured ratio and its uncertainty, and be willing to conclude it is not φ). Forced golden-ratio conclusions cost marks.

B: every variable, unit & photo scale defined
C: your own questions, not textbook material
D: reflection in every section (not just the end)
limits of one representative artifact weighed

nextStep: Reply with your two chosen artifacts and whether you can photograph the Newari window yourself. Then we finalize the research question and lock the exact mathematical techniques for each comparison.
